meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'As I began to love myself I found that anguish and emotional suffering are only warning signs'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Chaplin, and not a 70th-birthday speech. Wikiquote traces the line to Kim & Alison McMillen's 2001 book, via Portuguese.

answer.label: Not Charlie Chaplin — a re-translation of Kim McMillen
answer.authorDates: American writer · author of When I Loved Myself Enough (St. Martin’s Press, 2001)
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote lists this line among Chaplin’s misattributed quotations and identifies it as a re-translation, from Brazilian Portuguese, of text from When I Loved Myself Enough by Kim & Alison McMillen (2001) — not from any speech, book or letter of Chaplin’s. The popular framing, a “speech Charlie Chaplin gave on his 70th birthday,” has no documented source; Chaplin’s own office has stated flatly that he did not write it.
answer.confidenceText: No Chaplin speech, script, letter or memoir has ever been produced containing this wording; the traceable trail leads to a 2001 self-love book and a round trip through Portuguese.

source.excerpt: As I began to love myself I found that anguish and emotional suffering are only warning signs that I was living against my own truth. Today, I know, this is “AUTHENTICITY”.
trail: Wikiquote’s Charlie Chaplin page ↗ lists the exact sentence under Misattributed, calling it a re-translation from Portuguese-BR of text from When I Loved Myself Enough by Kim & Alison McMillen (2001).
Chaplin’s Office, quoted by a researcher who wrote to them, replied that the text was “NOT WRITTEN BY Charlie Chaplin” and comes from the McMillen book — read the exchange ↗.
The real book is easy to pin down: Open Library’s edition record ↗ gives When I Loved Myself Enough, St. Martin’s Press, 2001, 82 pages.

Its publisher describes the book as beginning “as one woman’s gift to the world, hand-made by Kim McMillen and handed out to friends,” with Alison continuing the work after Kim’s death — publisher page ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the circulating text as Wikiquote records it in Chaplin’s Misattributed section — a re-translation, not a passage from any Chaplin work and not McMillen’s published English.
source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted for this exact English wording, because its origin is an unsigned re-translation with no identifiable publication. The underlying work it derives from — Kim and Alison McMillen’s When I Loved Myself Enough, published by St. Martin’s Press in 2001 — is firmly in copyright, so this text should not be treated as public domain.

author.name: Kim McMillen
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: American writer · author of When I Loved Myself Enough (St. Martin's Press, 2001)
author.bio: Kim McMillen wrote short first-person reflections on self-acceptance, each beginning “When I loved myself enough…” The collection began, in her publisher’s words, as one woman’s gift to the world — handmade and handed out to friends. She did not live to see how far the words travelled; after her death her daughter Alison McMillen kept making the books and brought the manuscript to St. Martin’s Press, which published it in 2001.

cite.sourceCitation: Kim McMillen with Alison McMillen, When I Loved Myself Enough (New York: St. Martin's Press, 2001). The wording circulated as Chaplin's is an English re-translation of a Brazilian Portuguese version of that text; see “Charlie Chaplin,” Wikiquote, Misattributed section.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution, unpicked
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most-shared fake Chaplin texts — usually posted as a whole poem, “As I Began to Love Myself,” complete with a date and an occasion that no archive can corroborate.

items.why: Wikiquote places the line in its Misattributed section for Chaplin and explains it is “a re-translation (from Portuguese-BR) of a text from the book ‘When I Loved Myself Enough’ by Kim & Alison McMillen (2001)” — see the entry ↗.

items.who: A speech on his 70th birthday, 16 April 1959
items.why: Wikiquote attributes the “speech that Charlie Chaplin gave on his 70th birthday” framing to many sites and blogs, not to any documented record; no script, recording or press report of such a speech has been produced. Wikiquote ↗

The English sentence people share is not McMillen’s published English either — it is an unsigned translation back out of a Brazilian Portuguese rendering, which is why its rhythm and vocabulary match neither Chaplin nor the original book.

misattribution.truthLine: Chaplin’s own office has said it plainly: the text was not written by Charlie Chaplin and comes from Kim and Alison McMillen’s book — the office’s statement, quoted in full ↗.

context.heading: How a self-help booklet became a Chaplin speech
lead: The line belongs to a family of short reflections that all open the same way: When I loved myself enough… Kim McMillen wrote them as a private reckoning and gave them away as handmade booklets; after her death her daughter Alison kept producing them, and word of mouth carried the book to St. Martin’s Press, which published it in 2001.

The text was translated widely, and a Brazilian Portuguese version circulated hard on early blogs and email forwards. Somewhere in that circulation the author’s name fell off and Chaplin’s was pinned on — usually with the irresistible detail that he read it aloud on his 70th birthday. The English sentence people share today is a translation of that translation, which is why it reads nothing like Chaplin’s actual prose.
context.detailsSummary: Why the “70th birthday speech” detail should have been the tell
detailsBody: Chaplin was an unusually well-documented man: his films, scripts, correspondence and 1964 autobiography have been picked over by archivists for decades. A speech delivered on a famous birthday would be the easiest thing in the world to source — and no one ever has. Wikiquote notes the “70th birthday” framing comes from “many sites and blogs,” not from any record.

Chaplin’s office has answered the question directly, telling a researcher that the text was not written by him and comes from the McMillen book. That is about as close to a definitive denial as a quote investigation gets.
context.pull: The version in English is a translation of a translation — which is why nobody can find it in anything Chaplin wrote.
